chapter.title: Stream Processing
chapter.author: Martin Kleppmann
chapter.primary_goal: Understand how unbounded event streams are transmitted, stored, replayed, joined, windowed, converted into application state, and processed fault-tolerantly.

summary.overview: Chapter 11 generalizes batch processing from bounded files to unbounded event streams. It begins with messaging systems and the producer/consumer model, then contrasts traditional AMQP/JMS-style brokers with partitioned log-based brokers. Traditional brokers often assign individual messages to consumers, use acknowledgments and redelivery, and delete acknowledged messages. Log-based brokers instead retain messages on disk, partition topics, preserve order within a partition, and track consumer progress through offsets, making replay and fan-out natural. The chapter then connects streams to databases: a replication log is a stream of database writes, and change data capture can turn a database into a source of ordered change events for caches, search indexes, warehouses, and other derived systems. Event sourcing elevates the log to the application model itself, recording immutable domain events and deriving current state from them. This leads to a broader view in which mutable state is a materialized projection of an immutable event history. The chapter next examines stream-processing applications such as complex event processing, stream analytics, materialized-view maintenance, and search on streams. Reasoning about time is difficult because event time and processing time differ, events may arrive late or out of order, and windows may need corrections. It defines tumbling, hopping, sliding, and session windows. Stream joins are categorized as stream-stream, stream-table, and table-table joins, all of which require maintained state and raise questions about event ordering and time-dependent reference data. Finally, fault tolerance is explored through microbatching, checkpointing, internal atomic commit, idempotent writes, and state reconstruction. The goal is effectively exactly-once visible results despite retries and failures.

learning_objectives.objective: Explain bounded batch input versus unbounded stream input.
Define events, producers, consumers, topics, and streams.
Explain drop, buffer, and backpressure strategies for slow consumers.
Compare direct messaging with brokered messaging.
Compare message brokers with databases.
Distinguish load balancing from fan-out.
Explain acknowledgments, redelivery, and message reordering.
Explain the design of partitioned log-based brokers.
Explain offsets and replay in a partitioned log.
Explain why dual writes can permanently diverge.
Explain change data capture and derived-data consumers.
Explain consistent snapshots and CDC log positions.
Explain log compaction and tombstones.
Distinguish CDC from event sourcing.
Explain command validation before immutable event creation.
Explain mutable state as a projection of immutable events.
Explain advantages and limits of immutable event histories.
Explain CQRS as separate write and read representations.
Describe major uses of stream processing.
Distinguish CEP from stream analytics.
Explain event time versus processing time.
Explain how to handle straggler/late events.
Compare tumbling, hopping, sliding, and session windows.
Compare stream-stream, stream-table, and table-table joins.
Explain time-dependent joins and slowly changing dimensions.
Define exactly-once/effectively-once semantics in stream processing.
Compare microbatching and rolling checkpoints.
Explain why external side effects complicate exactly-once guarantees.
Explain idempotence and offset-based deduplication.
Explain state recovery through snapshots, changelogs, or replay.

bounded_vs_unbounded.batch: Operates on a known finite input and can know when it has finished.
bounded_vs_unbounded.stream: Operates continuously on data incrementally arriving over time; the input has no natural end.

event.definition: A small immutable record describing something that happened.
event.typical_fields: Payload plus a timestamp describing when the event occurred.

producer_consumer_topic.topic: Groups related events in a stream.

slow_consumer_strategies.backpressure: Block or slow producers until consumers catch up.

direct_messaging.strength: Can provide very low latency and simple direct delivery.
direct_messaging.limitation: Producer/consumer availability and message-loss handling are often pushed into application logic.

message_broker.definition: A server optimized for storing and forwarding message streams between producers and consumers.

broker_vs_database.retention: Traditional brokers often delete messages after successful delivery; databases retain until explicitly deleted.
broker_vs_database.query_model: Databases support arbitrary queries/indexes; brokers mainly support subscriptions/topics.
broker_vs_database.notification: Brokers actively notify consumers of new data; database queries usually return a point-in-time snapshot.

consumer_patterns.load_balancing: Each message goes to one consumer in a consumer group.
consumer_patterns.fan_out: Each message goes independently to every subscribed consumer/group.
consumer_patterns.combined: Multiple independent groups can each receive the full stream while load-balancing inside each group.

acknowledgment_redelivery.ack: Consumer tells broker that processing completed.
acknowledgment_redelivery.redelivery: If ack is missing due to crash/timeout, broker sends message again.
acknowledgment_redelivery.duplicate_risk: Message may have been processed even if acknowledgment was lost.
acknowledgment_redelivery.reordering: Load balancing plus redelivery can change processing order.

partitioned_log.storage: Append-only sequence of messages stored on disk.
partitioned_log.topic: A group of independent partitions carrying the same type of events.
partitioned_log.ordering: Total order inside a partition; no global order across partitions.

log_consumer_groups.fanout: Independent consumers can reread the same retained log.
log_consumer_groups.load_balance: Partitions, rather than individual messages, are assigned to consumer nodes.
log_consumer_groups.parallelism_limit: A consumer group normally cannot use more active consumers than topic partitions.
log_consumer_groups.head_of_line: One slow message stalls later messages in that partition.

consumer_offsets.meaning: All messages before the offset are considered processed; later offsets are not yet processed.
consumer_offsets.recovery: After consumer failure, another node resumes from the last checkpointed offset.
consumer_offsets.duplicate_case: Messages processed after the last saved offset may be processed again after failover.

log_retention.segments: Old log segments are deleted or archived.
log_retention.buffer: A retained log acts like a large disk-backed circular buffer.
log_retention.slow_consumer: If it falls behind beyond retention, it misses old messages.

replay.mechanism: Consumer can reset or use an older offset and reread historical messages.
replay.benefit: Experimentation, debugging, recovery, and rebuilding derived data.

database_as_stream.replication_log: A stream of database write events.
database_as_stream.state_machine: Replicas processing identical deterministic events in the same order converge to the same state.

dual_write_problem.race: Two systems can observe concurrent writes in different orders and permanently disagree.
dual_write_problem.partial_failure: One write can succeed while another fails.
dual_write_problem.lesson: Independent dual writes do not provide atomicity or a shared ordering.

cdc.definition: Observe database changes and expose them as a stream for replication to other systems.
cdc.leader_follower_view: The source database acts as leader; derived systems consume the ordered changelog as followers.
cdc.async: System of record usually commits without waiting for derived consumers.

cdc_implementation.triggers: Possible but often fragile and costly.
cdc_implementation.replication_log: Parsing WAL/binlog/oplog can be more robust but must handle schema changes.

initial_snapshot.need: A new derived system requires existing state plus subsequent changes.
initial_snapshot.rule: Snapshot must correspond to a known offset in the change log.

log_compaction.method: Keep the newest value per key and discard superseded values.
log_compaction.tombstone: Special null/deletion record removes a key during compaction.
log_compaction.benefit: Compacted log can reconstruct current database contents without retaining all overwrites.

event_sourcing.definition: Application explicitly records domain-level immutable events as the system's write model.
event_sourcing.difference_from_cdc: CDC extracts low-level database mutations from a mutable DB; event sourcing makes immutable domain events explicit in application logic.

derived_current_state.need: Users usually want current state, not the raw history.
derived_current_state.method: Deterministically fold/replay events into a read model or snapshot.
derived_current_state.event_history: Unlike compactable CDC state updates, event-sourced domain events often must all be retained because later events do not overwrite earlier facts.

command_vs_event.command: A request that may be rejected during validation.
command_vs_event.event: A durable immutable fact produced only after acceptance.
command_vs_event.rule: Consumers cannot reject an event after it is part of the log.

state_and_streams.relationship: Mutable state is the accumulated result of a sequence of immutable events.
state_and_streams.analogy: State is the integral of an event stream; a change stream is the derivative of state.
state_and_streams.system_of_record: If the event log is durable, mutable state can be treated as derived/cache-like data.

immutable_event_advantages.auditability: Original facts remain available; corrections can be represented by compensating events.
immutable_event_advantages.debuggability: Can reconstruct why the system reached a state.
immutable_event_advantages.analytics: Preserves information erased from current state.
immutable_event_advantages.multiple_views: Same log can feed multiple read models.

cqrs.name: Command Query Responsibility Segregation
cqrs.idea: Separate the representation optimized for writes from one or more representations optimized for reads.

eventual_read_view.problem: Asynchronous consumers may cause read-your-own-write lag.
eventual_read_view.stronger_option: Update event log and read model synchronously/transactionally, or use stronger ordered coordination.

serial_partition_processing.benefit: If log and state are partitioned identically, one single-threaded consumer per partition can avoid write concurrency control by processing events serially.

immutability_limits.storage: High-churn histories may become very large and make compaction/GC important.
immutability_limits.deletion: Privacy, legal, or security requirements may require actual historical deletion.
immutability_limits.difficulty: Copies may remain in filesystems, SSDs, backups, and other storage layers.

options: Transform input streams into derived output streams

cep.definition: Long-lived queries/rules search a continuous stream for event patterns.
cep.database_reversal: Queries remain stored; incoming events flow past them.

stream_analytics.focus: Aggregations/statistics rather than specific event sequences.
stream_analytics.window: A finite time interval over which aggregation is calculated.
stream_analytics.approximation: Bloom filters, HyperLogLog, and percentile approximations reduce memory; streaming itself is not inherently approximate.

materialized_view_maintenance.definition: Continuously update an efficiently queryable derived view as source events change.
materialized_view_maintenance.long_history: Unlike short analytics windows, some materialized views conceptually depend on history extending to the beginning of time.

search_on_streams.idea: Store queries and continuously match incoming documents/events against them.
search_on_streams.contrast: Conventional search indexes documents then runs transient queries; stream search keeps queries and sends documents past them.

stream_vs_actor.actor: Concurrency/distributed-execution abstraction; communication often ephemeral and point-to-point.
stream_vs_actor.stream: Data-management abstraction; logs are durable, multi-subscriber, and pipelines are often acyclic.

event_time_processing_time.event_time: Timestamp describing when the underlying event actually occurred.
event_time_processing_time.processing_time: Local time when stream processor handles the event.
event_time_processing_time.risk: Backlogs/restarts/replay can make processing-time windows create false spikes or incorrect results.

out_of_order_events.cause: Network delays, queueing, different producers, restarts, replay.
out_of_order_events.fact: Events can arrive in an order different from the order they occurred.

late_events.problem: A processor cannot know with certainty that no more events for an event-time window will arrive.
options: Ignore late events and monitor drops

clock_uncertainty_in_events.mobile_case: Offline devices may send events hours/days after occurrence and device clocks may be wrong.
clock_uncertainty_in_events.offset_estimate: Compare device send time with server receive time to estimate clock offset.

windows.tumbling: Fixed, non-overlapping; each event belongs to exactly one.
windows.hopping: Fixed length, overlapping, with a smaller hop interval.
windows.sliding: Contains events within a relative interval of each other rather than fixed boundaries.
windows.session: No fixed duration; closes after inactivity.

stream_stream_join.example: Search event joined with click event by session ID.
stream_stream_join.state: Maintain recent events for the join window and emit matched/unmatched results.

stream_table_join.example: Activity event joined with user profile.
stream_table_join.local_state: Keep a local copy/index of table data and update it through a CDC changelog.
stream_table_join.conceptual_window: Table side has a window reaching back to the beginning of time, with newer versions replacing older ones.

table_table_join.use: Maintain a materialized join view as either base table changes.
table_table_join.twitter_example: Tweets and follow relationships jointly maintain home timelines.

time_dependent_join.problem: Which version of changing reference state should an event join against?
time_dependent_join.example: Tax rate valid at the time of sale.
time_dependent_join.nondeterminism: Unspecified interleaving across streams can produce different results on replay.
time_dependent_join.scd: Slowly changing dimensions may use version identifiers to make historical joins deterministic.
time_dependent_join.cost: Retaining all versions prevents ordinary compaction of old reference-state versions.

exactly_once.chapter_preference: Effectively-once is a more descriptive term.
exactly_once.meaning: Visible result should be as if each input record affected output once, even if internal retries reprocess it.

microbatching.method: Break stream into small batches and process each as a miniature batch job.
microbatching.tradeoff: Smaller batches increase scheduling overhead; larger batches increase output latency.

checkpointing.method: Periodically snapshot operator state to durable storage using barriers; restart from latest checkpoint.
checkpointing.advantage: Does not force processing window size to equal checkpoint interval.

external_side_effects.problem: Framework can discard/retry its own state, but cannot retract an already-sent email or arbitrary external DB effect.

atomic_commit_streaming.goal: Input acknowledgment/offset, state changes, output messages, and external writes must commit together or not at all.
atomic_commit_streaming.restricted_framework: Efficient transactions are easier when messaging and state are managed inside one stream-processing environment.

idempotence.definition: Repeating the same operation has the same final effect as performing it once.
idempotence.idempotent_example: Set key to a fixed value.
idempotence.dedupe: Store source message offset/identifier with output and skip already-applied updates.
assumptions: Replay same messages in same order

state_recovery.remote: Keep state in a replicated remote datastore, at possible per-message latency cost.
state_recovery.local_snapshot: Keep local state and periodically replicate/checkpoint it.
state_recovery.changelog: Replicate state changes to a compacted log.
state_recovery.replay: Rebuild state by replaying input events if affordable.

flashcards.front: What is the defining difference between batch and stream input?
flashcards.back: Batch input is bounded; stream input is unbounded and incrementally arrives over time.

flashcards.front: Why do batch systems artificially divide real-world data into time chunks?
flashcards.back: Real-world data often never ends, but batch jobs require finite inputs.

flashcards.front: What does stream processing try to reduce compared with daily batch jobs?
flashcards.back: The delay between an input change and its effect on output.

flashcards.front: What is an event?
flashcards.back: A small self-contained immutable record describing something that happened.

flashcards.front: What does an event usually include?
flashcards.back: A timestamp plus encoded details/payload.

flashcards.front: What is a producer?
flashcards.back: A node/application that generates or publishes events.

flashcards.front: What is a consumer?
flashcards.back: A node/application that subscribes to and processes events.

flashcards.front: What is a topic/stream?
flashcards.back: A logical grouping of related events.

flashcards.front: Why is frequent polling inefficient?
flashcards.back: Most polls may return no new data, creating overhead.

flashcards.front: What is preferable to frequent polling for low latency?
flashcards.back: Notify/push events to consumers when new data appears.

flashcards.front: Three responses to producers outrunning consumers?
flashcards.back: Drop messages, buffer them, or apply backpressure.

flashcards.front: What is backpressure?
flashcards.back: Blocking/slowing producers when downstream buffers are full.

flashcards.front: What do Unix pipes and TCP use for overload?
flashcards.back: Backpressure with bounded buffers.

flashcards.front: What durability tradeoff exists in messaging?
flashcards.back: Disk/replication improves durability but costs throughput/latency.

flashcards.front: When may message loss be acceptable?
flashcards.back: For periodic sensor/metric samples where later values replace missing ones.

flashcards.front: When is message loss particularly harmful?
flashcards.back: When counting events, because each lost event makes counts wrong.

flashcards.front: What is direct messaging?
flashcards.back: Producer sends directly to consumer without an intermediary broker.

flashcards.front: Examples of direct messaging?
flashcards.back: UDP multicast, ZeroMQ/nanomsg, StatsD, HTTP/RPC webhooks.

flashcards.front: Main limitation of direct messaging?
flashcards.back: Clients often must stay online and application code must handle loss/retry.

flashcards.front: What is a message broker?
flashcards.back: A server/database-like system optimized for receiving, storing, and forwarding message streams.

flashcards.front: Why can brokers tolerate clients coming and going?
flashcards.back: Messages are centralized at the broker rather than held only at producers/consumers.

flashcards.front: What does a producer normally wait for with an asynchronous broker?
flashcards.back: Confirmation that the broker accepted/buffered the message, not consumer completion.

flashcards.front: How do traditional brokers differ from databases in retention?
flashcards.back: They often delete messages after successful delivery.

flashcards.front: How do databases differ in query capability?
flashcards.back: They support arbitrary queries/indexes; brokers primarily expose subscriptions/topics.

flashcards.front: How do brokers differ from normal DB queries in notification?
flashcards.back: Brokers notify consumers when new data arrives.

flashcards.front: What is load balancing in messaging?
flashcards.back: Each message is delivered to one consumer within a group.

flashcards.front: What is fan-out?
flashcards.back: Each message is delivered to all independent subscribers/groups.

flashcards.front: Can fan-out and load balancing be combined?
flashcards.back: Yes; every consumer group gets all messages, while group members share work.

flashcards.front: Why do brokers require acknowledgments?
flashcards.back: To know a message was processed before deleting/advancing it.

flashcards.front: What happens if no acknowledgment arrives?
flashcards.back: Broker assumes processing failed and redelivers.

flashcards.front: Can redelivery create duplicates?
flashcards.back: Yes, if processing succeeded but the acknowledgment was lost.

flashcards.front: How can load balancing plus redelivery affect order?
flashcards.back: An older unacked message can be redelivered after a newer message.

flashcards.front: When is message reordering harmless?
flashcards.back: When messages are independent and have no causal dependency.

flashcards.front: What is a partitioned log?
flashcards.back: An append-only message log divided into independent partitions.

flashcards.front: How does a log-based producer send a message?
flashcards.back: Append it to the end of a log partition.

flashcards.front: How does a consumer receive log messages?
flashcards.back: Sequentially read from the log.

flashcards.front: What Unix command resembles log consumption?
flashcards.back: tail -f.

flashcards.front: Why partition a log?
flashcards.back: To scale throughput across multiple disks/machines.

flashcards.front: What is an offset?
flashcards.back: Monotonically increasing sequence number of a message within a partition.

flashcards.front: What ordering is guaranteed in a partitioned log?
flashcards.back: Total order within each partition, not across partitions.

flashcards.front: Examples of log-based brokers in the chapter?
flashcards.back: Kafka, Amazon Kinesis Streams, Twitter DistributedLog.

flashcards.front: How do log brokers support fan-out?
flashcards.back: Multiple consumers independently read the retained log.

flashcards.front: How is load balancing done in a log consumer group?
flashcards.back: Assign entire partitions to consumer nodes.

flashcards.front: What's the usual maximum number of active consumers per group?
flashcards.back: At most the number of partitions.

flashcards.front: What is head-of-line blocking in a log partition?
flashcards.back: One slow message delays all later messages in the same partition.

flashcards.front: When is traditional JMS/AMQP style preferable?
flashcards.back: Expensive per-message processing, message-level parallelism desired, ordering less important.

flashcards.front: When is log-based style preferable?
flashcards.back: High throughput, fast per-message processing, and ordering matters.

flashcards.front: What does a consumer offset summarize?
flashcards.back: Everything before it has been processed; later messages have not.

flashcards.front: Why are offsets cheaper than per-message acknowledgments?
flashcards.back: The broker only needs to checkpoint progress periodically.

flashcards.front: What happens after consumer failover?
flashcards.back: Another node resumes from the last stored offset.

flashcards.front: What causes duplicate processing after failover?
flashcards.back: Messages processed after the last checkpointed offset are replayed.

flashcards.front: How does a retained log reclaim disk space?
flashcards.back: Delete/archive old segments.

flashcards.front: What happens if a consumer falls behind retention?
flashcards.back: It misses messages whose segments were deleted.

flashcards.front: What type of buffer is a retained log like?
flashcards.back: Large disk-backed circular/ring buffer.

flashcards.front: Why is log throughput relatively stable as retention grows?
flashcards.back: Messages are written to disk regardless of current backlog size.

flashcards.front: What should operators monitor for slow consumers?
flashcards.back: Lag behind the head of the log.

flashcards.front: Does one slow log consumer disrupt other consumers?
flashcards.back: Generally no; consumers are independent.

flashcards.front: What is replay?
flashcards.back: Reset/use an earlier consumer offset to reread old events.

flashcards.front: Why is replay powerful?
flashcards.back: It supports experimentation, debugging, recovery, and rebuilding outputs.

flashcards.front: Why is log consumption non-destructive?
flashcards.back: Reading does not delete the message from the log.

flashcards.front: How is a DB replication log like a stream?
flashcards.back: It is an ordered sequence of database write events.

flashcards.front: What does state machine replication require?
flashcards.back: Replicas process the same deterministic events in the same order.

flashcards.front: Why do applications need to synchronize multiple systems?
flashcards.back: Same logical data may live in OLTP DBs, caches, search indexes, and warehouses.

flashcards.front: What is a dual write?
flashcards.back: Application explicitly writes the same logical change to multiple systems.

flashcards.front: How can dual writes race?
flashcards.back: Two systems may receive concurrent writes in opposite orders.

flashcards.front: What can a dual-write failure do?
flashcards.back: One system updates while another does not, causing inconsistency.

flashcards.front: What is CDC?
flashcards.back: Change data capture: exposing database changes as a stream for other systems.

flashcards.front: What role does the source DB play in CDC?
flashcards.back: Leader/system of record.

flashcards.front: What role do search/cache/warehouse consumers play?
flashcards.back: Derived follower-like systems.

flashcards.front: Why is a log broker good for CDC?
flashcards.back: It preserves ordered changes and decouples slow consumers.

flashcards.front: Why are DB triggers often weak CDC mechanisms?
flashcards.back: They can be fragile and have performance overhead.

flashcards.front: What lower-level logs can CDC parse?
flashcards.back: WAL/binlog/oplog depending on database.

flashcards.front: Is CDC usually synchronous?
flashcards.back: No, usually asynchronous.

flashcards.front: What downside follows asynchronous CDC?
flashcards.back: Replication lag.

flashcards.front: Why does a new derived system need an initial snapshot?
flashcards.back: Recent changes alone do not contain unchanged historical records.

flashcards.front: What must a CDC snapshot correspond to?
flashcards.back: A known offset/position in the change log.

flashcards.front: What is log compaction?
flashcards.back: Keep latest value per key and discard superseded versions.

flashcards.front: What is a tombstone?
flashcards.back: A special deletion marker used during compaction.

flashcards.front: What determines compacted-log space?
flashcards.back: Current key set/state rather than all historical writes.

flashcards.front: How can a compacted log rebuild a derived system?
flashcards.back: Consume from the beginning to obtain the latest retained value for every key.

flashcards.front: What is event sourcing?
flashcards.back: Application-level modeling where immutable domain events are the primary write history.

flashcards.front: CDC vs event sourcing?
flashcards.back: CDC extracts low-level DB mutations; event sourcing explicitly writes domain-level immutable events.

flashcards.front: Why is event sourcing useful for application evolution?
flashcards.back: Events preserve intent and can drive new derived behavior later.

flashcards.front: Why isn't an event log alone enough for a UI?
flashcards.back: Users need current state, not just the raw change history.

flashcards.front: How is current state built from event sourcing?
flashcards.back: Deterministically replay/fold events into a read model.

flashcards.front: Can event-sourced logs usually be compacted like CDC logs?
flashcards.back: Not in the same way, because older domain events remain meaningful facts.

flashcards.front: Why use event-sourced snapshots?
flashcards.back: Speed up reads/recovery without changing the authoritative event history.

flashcards.front: What is a command?
flashcards.back: A requested action that may still be rejected.

flashcards.front: What is an event?
flashcards.back: An accepted durable immutable fact.

flashcards.front: When must command validation occur?
flashcards.back: Before the command becomes an immutable event.

flashcards.front: Can an event-stream consumer reject an already-published event?
flashcards.back: No.

flashcards.front: How can async validation be represented?
flashcards.back: Tentative event followed by confirmation or rejection-related event.

flashcards.front: How are mutable state and immutable events related?
flashcards.back: Current state is the accumulated result of past events.

flashcards.front: Mathematical analogy for state and events?
flashcards.back: State is the integral of events; a change stream is the derivative of state.

flashcards.front: What does 'the truth is the log' mean?
flashcards.back: The log is durable history; current database state is a derived/latest-value view.

flashcards.front: Why are immutable events good for auditing?
flashcards.back: Corrections can be appended without erasing original facts.

flashcards.front: Why are immutable events useful for analytics?
flashcards.back: They preserve actions that current state may no longer reveal.

flashcards.front: What can be derived from one event log?
flashcards.back: Multiple independent read-optimized views.

flashcards.front: What is CQRS?
flashcards.back: Separating write representation from read/query representation.

flashcards.front: Why can CQRS ease schema/view evolution?
flashcards.back: New read models can be built alongside old ones from the same event log.

flashcards.front: Main downside of async derived views?
flashcards.back: A user may not immediately read their own write.

flashcards.front: How can synchronous read-view updates be achieved?
flashcards.back: Atomic transaction/strong ordered coordination between log and read view.

flashcards.front: How can event sourcing simplify concurrency?
flashcards.back: A user action can become one atomic log append rather than many direct state writes.

flashcards.front: When can single-threaded consumers avoid write concurrency control?
flashcards.back: When event log and application state use the same partitioning and each event touches one partition.

flashcards.front: Why can immutable history become expensive?
flashcards.back: High update/delete churn creates large histories and compaction/GC overhead.

flashcards.front: Why may immutable systems still need deletion?
flashcards.back: Privacy, data-protection, or sensitive-data requirements.

flashcards.front: Why is true deletion difficult?
flashcards.back: Copies may survive in filesystems, SSDs, backups, and other layers.

flashcards.front: Three broad outputs of a stream processor?
flashcards.back: Write state, notify humans, or produce derived streams.

flashcards.front: Why can't a stream processor restart from the beginning after every failure?
flashcards.back: A stream may have been running for years and never ends.

flashcards.front: What is CEP?
flashcards.back: Complex event processing: continuously match streams against stored event-pattern queries.

flashcards.front: How does CEP invert normal database querying?
flashcards.back: Queries are persistent and events flow past them.

flashcards.front: What does stream analytics focus on?
flashcards.back: Aggregations/statistical metrics over many events.

flashcards.front: Examples of stream metrics?
flashcards.back: Event rate, rolling averages, time comparisons, percentiles.

flashcards.front: What is a window?
flashcards.back: A time interval over which stream events are aggregated.

flashcards.front: Does use of approximate algorithms mean stream processing is inherently approximate?
flashcards.back: No.

flashcards.front: Why use Bloom filters/HyperLogLog in streams?
flashcards.back: Approximate results can use much less memory.

flashcards.front: What is materialized-view maintenance?
flashcards.back: Continuously update a derived queryable state as source changes arrive.

flashcards.front: How long may a materialized-view history window be?
flashcards.back: Conceptually all the way back to the beginning of time.

flashcards.front: What is search on streams?
flashcards.back: Store queries and continuously match incoming events/documents against them.

flashcards.front: How is stream search opposite normal search?
flashcards.back: Normal search stores/indexes documents then runs transient queries; stream search stores queries and sends documents past them.

flashcards.front: Actor systems vs stream processors?
flashcards.back: Actors focus on concurrency/communication; stream processors focus on durable dataflow.

flashcards.front: Why is time reasoning hard in streams?
flashcards.back: Processing time may differ greatly from event occurrence time.

flashcards.front: What is event time?
flashcards.back: When the event actually occurred according to its embedded timestamp.

flashcards.front: What is processing time?
flashcards.back: When the processor handled the event.

flashcards.front: Why can processing-time windows be misleading after restart?
flashcards.back: Backlogged events are processed quickly, appearing as an artificial spike.

flashcards.front: Why can events arrive out of order?
flashcards.back: Different servers, network delays, queueing, restarts, and replay.

flashcards.front: What is the late-event problem?
flashcards.back: You cannot be certain all events for an event-time window have arrived.

flashcards.front: Two strategies for stragglers?
flashcards.back: Ignore/drop with monitoring, or publish a correction/retraction.

flashcards.front: How can producers sometimes signal event-time progress?
flashcards.back: Emit a message saying no future event will have timestamp earlier than t.

flashcards.front: Why are mobile event timestamps tricky?
flashcards.back: Events may be delayed offline and device clocks may be wrong.

flashcards.front: What three timestamps can help correct device clocks?
flashcards.back: Device event time, device send time, server receive time.

flashcards.front: What is a tumbling window?
flashcards.back: Fixed-length non-overlapping windows; each event belongs to exactly one.

flashcards.front: What is a hopping window?
flashcards.back: Fixed-length overlapping windows advanced by a hop interval.

flashcards.front: What is a sliding window?
flashcards.back: Events are grouped by relative temporal proximity rather than fixed boundaries.

flashcards.front: What is a session window?
flashcards.back: Variable-length window ending after a period of inactivity.

flashcards.front: Three stream join categories?
flashcards.back: Stream-stream, stream-table, table-table.

flashcards.front: What is a stream-stream/window join?
flashcards.back: Join related events from streams within a bounded time window.

flashcards.front: Example stream-stream join?
flashcards.back: Search event with later click event by session ID.

flashcards.front: What state does a stream-stream join need?
flashcards.back: Recent events indexed by join key for the chosen window.

flashcards.front: What is a stream-table join?
flashcards.back: Enrich each stream event using current state from a table/local replica.

flashcards.front: How can stream-table join avoid remote DB lookups?
flashcards.back: Maintain a local copy/index of the table.

flashcards.front: How does local table copy stay current?
flashcards.back: Consume its CDC changelog.

flashcards.front: Conceptual window of the table side?
flashcards.back: From beginning of time, with newer versions replacing older ones.

flashcards.front: What is a table-table join in streaming?
flashcards.back: Continuously maintain a materialized join as either input table changes.

flashcards.front: Twitter timeline example requires streams of what?
flashcards.back: Tweet changes and follow/unfollow relationship changes.

flashcards.front: Why are stream joins time-dependent?
flashcards.back: Reference state changes, and processing order across streams determines which version is used.

flashcards.front: Tax-rate example illustrates what?
flashcards.back: Historical event should join with the tax-rate version valid at event time.

flashcards.front: What is a slowly changing dimension approach?
flashcards.back: Give each version of reference data a unique identifier and join historical facts to that version.

flashcards.front: Why can SCD versioning conflict with compaction?
flashcards.back: Historical versions must be retained.

flashcards.front: What does exactly-once mean here?
flashcards.back: Visible output is as if each input record took effect once despite possible retries.

flashcards.front: Why is 'effectively-once' more accurate?
flashcards.back: Records may actually be processed multiple times internally.

flashcards.front: What is microbatching?
flashcards.back: Treat small chunks of a stream as miniature batch jobs.

flashcards.front: Which system is cited for microbatching?
flashcards.back: Spark Streaming.

flashcards.front: Microbatch size tradeoff?
flashcards.back: Smaller = more coordination overhead; larger = more output latency.

flashcards.front: What does Flink-style checkpointing do?
flashcards.back: Periodically persist operator state and resume from the latest checkpoint after failure.

flashcards.front: Why don't checkpointing/microbatching alone solve external side effects?
flashcards.back: Already-emitted external effects cannot simply be discarded during retry.

flashcards.front: What must atomic stream processing coordinate?
flashcards.back: State, downstream outputs, external writes, and input acknowledgments/offsets.

flashcards.front: What is idempotence?
flashcards.back: Repeating an operation has the same final effect as doing it once.

flashcards.front: Idempotent example?
flashcards.back: Set a key to a fixed value.

flashcards.front: Non-idempotent example?
flashcards.back: Increment a counter.

flashcards.front: How can offsets make writes idempotent?
flashcards.back: Store the triggering offset with output and ignore an offset already applied.

flashcards.front: What assumptions support offset-based idempotence?
flashcards.back: Same replay order, deterministic processing, no concurrent conflicting writer, possible fencing.

flashcards.front: Why might fencing be needed after processor failover?
flashcards.back: A supposedly dead old processor may still be alive and writing.

flashcards.front: What state must stream processors recover?
flashcards.back: Window aggregates, join indexes/tables, and other operator state.

flashcards.front: State recovery option 1?
flashcards.back: Remote replicated datastore.

flashcards.front: State recovery option 2?
flashcards.back: Local state plus periodic durable snapshot/checkpoint.

flashcards.front: State recovery option 3?
flashcards.back: Replicate state changes to a compacted changelog.

flashcards.front: State recovery option 4?
flashcards.back: Rebuild from replaying input events.

flashcards.front: How does Flink restore state in the cited approach?
flashcards.back: Snapshots operator state to durable storage such as HDFS.

flashcards.front: How do Samza/Kafka Streams replicate state?
flashcards.back: Send state changes to a compacted Kafka topic.

flashcards.front: When is replay-based rebuilding practical?
flashcards.back: When state covers a short enough window or log-based source can cheaply recreate it.

flashcards.front: Is local or remote state universally better?
flashcards.back: No; tradeoffs depend on storage/network performance.

flashcards.front: Traditional AMQP/JMS broker ideal use in summary?
flashcards.back: Asynchronous RPC/task queue where ordering and replay are less important.

flashcards.front: Log-based broker ideal use in summary?
flashcards.back: Ordered high-throughput streaming with partition offsets and replay.

flashcards.front: What does database-as-stream enable?
flashcards.back: Continuously keep caches, search indexes, analytics, and other derived systems up to date.

flashcards.front: What three join categories does the summary reiterate?
flashcards.back: Stream-stream, stream-table, table-table.

flashcards.front: What fault-tolerance techniques does the summary list?
flashcards.back: Microbatching, checkpointing, transactions, and idempotent writes.

scenario_questions.scenario: A producer sends 100k events/sec but consumers handle 50k/sec.
scenario_questions.question: What three broad strategies exist?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Drop, buffer, or apply backpressure.

scenario_questions.scenario: A consumer processed a task but crashed before sending its acknowledgment.
scenario_questions.question: What can happen?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Broker redelivers it, so the task may execute twice.

scenario_questions.scenario: A traditional queue load-balances m3 and m4; m3 worker crashes.
scenario_questions.question: Can order change?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Yes. m4 may finish before redelivered m3.

scenario_questions.scenario: A Kafka-like topic has 12 partitions and 20 consumers in one group.
scenario_questions.question: How many can normally process partitions at once?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: At most 12; extra group members are idle.

scenario_questions.scenario: Consumer saves offset 100, processes through 110, then crashes before checkpointing.
scenario_questions.question: What happens after failover?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Messages 101-110 may be processed again.

scenario_questions.scenario: A new analytics experiment needs to reprocess last week's events.
scenario_questions.question: Which broker design makes this easy?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A retained log-based broker with resettable offsets.

scenario_questions.scenario: Two app instances dual-write DB and search index in opposite interleavings.
scenario_questions.question: What can result?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Permanent divergence even though every individual write succeeded.

scenario_questions.scenario: You add a new search index to a CDC pipeline but only retain 24 hours of changes.
scenario_questions.question: What else do you need?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A consistent source snapshot tied to a known changelog offset, unless a compacted full-state log can rebuild it.

scenario_questions.scenario: A user changes the same profile 1 million times.
scenario_questions.question: How does compacted CDC reduce history?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: It eventually retains only the newest value for that key, plus possibly temporary older segments.

scenario_questions.scenario: You want to know not only current shopping cart contents but every add/remove decision.
scenario_questions.question: CDC current-state compaction or event sourcing?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Event sourcing better preserves domain-level action history.

scenario_questions.scenario: A seat-reservation request violates uniqueness.
scenario_questions.question: Should it become an event first?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: No. Validate the command synchronously before publishing the immutable reservation event, or model tentative/confirmation events.

scenario_questions.scenario: A user posts an event and immediately queries an asynchronously maintained read model.
scenario_questions.question: What issue may appear?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Read-your-own-write lag.

scenario_questions.scenario: A stream processor detects sequences matching 'failed login, failed login, successful admin login'.
scenario_questions.question: Which category?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Complex event processing.

scenario_questions.scenario: A service computes 5-minute p99 latency continuously.
scenario_questions.question: Which category?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Stream analytics using a time window.

scenario_questions.scenario: A processor is down for one minute and then rapidly drains backlog.
scenario_questions.question: Why is processing-time request rate misleading?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: The backlog looks like a traffic spike even if real event-time traffic was steady.

scenario_questions.scenario: A one-minute event-time window is already emitted, then a delayed event arrives.
scenario_questions.question: Two choices?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Drop/monitor it or emit a corrected/retracted window result.

scenario_questions.scenario: A mobile device is offline for six hours before uploading events.
scenario_questions.question: Why can server receive time be misleading?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: It describes upload time, not the original user interaction time.

scenario_questions.scenario: You need rolling 5-minute metrics updated every minute.
scenario_questions.question: Which window?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Hopping window: length 5 minutes, hop 1 minute.

scenario_questions.scenario: You want sessions that end after 30 minutes of inactivity.
scenario_questions.question: Which window?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Session window.

scenario_questions.scenario: Search events and click events must match within one hour by session ID.
scenario_questions.question: Which join?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Stream-stream/window join.

scenario_questions.scenario: A clickstream must be enriched with the latest user profile without remote DB request per event.
scenario_questions.question: Design?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Maintain a local profile table and update it from CDC; perform a stream-table join locally.

scenario_questions.scenario: A home timeline cache updates when tweets or follow relationships change.
scenario_questions.question: Which join?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Table-table join/materialized-view maintenance.

scenario_questions.scenario: Historical invoices are replayed after a tax-rate change.
scenario_questions.question: Which rate should be used?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: The tax-rate version valid at sale time, potentially identified using SCD versioning.

scenario_questions.scenario: A Spark Streaming operator fails after emitting a nontransactional email.
scenario_questions.question: Can microbatch retry alone ensure once-only email?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: No. The external side effect may be repeated.

scenario_questions.scenario: A consumer writes 'balance=100' twice due to retry.
scenario_questions.question: Is the operation idempotent?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Yes, setting the same fixed value has the same final state.

scenario_questions.scenario: A consumer increments a counter twice after replay.
scenario_questions.question: Idempotent?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: No; the counter changes twice.

scenario_questions.scenario: A consumer stores Kafka offset 908 with a DB row and later replays offset 908.
scenario_questions.question: How can it avoid duplicate effect?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Detect that offset 908 was already applied and skip/reconcile the duplicate.

scenario_questions.scenario: A stream operator loses local window state.
scenario_questions.question: How can it recover?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Restore a durable checkpoint/changelog or replay the needed input window.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is streaming not merely 'batch but faster'?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Streams are unbounded, so operations such as global sort, end-of-job publication, and restart-from-beginning fault recovery no longer directly apply.

short_answer_questions.question: Traditional broker vs log broker?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Traditional brokers assign/ack/delete individual messages and suit task queues; log brokers retain ordered partition logs, checkpoint offsets, support replay, and suit derived stream processing.

short_answer_questions.question: Why can acknowledgments still lead to duplicates?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: The consumer may finish processing but its ack can be lost, causing the broker to redeliver.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is ordering per partition rather than global in log brokers?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Each partition is an independent append-only log; offsets totally order messages only inside that log.

short_answer_questions.question: Why are consumer offsets powerful?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: They compact progress tracking into one number per partition and let consumers restart, replay, or move backward through retained history.

short_answer_questions.question: Why are dual writes unsafe?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: No shared atomic ordering spans both systems; races can reorder writes and partial failure can update only one destination.

short_answer_questions.question: How does CDC solve system synchronization?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Treat source DB's ordered changelog as authoritative and have derived systems consume changes in that same order.

short_answer_questions.question: Initial snapshot vs log compaction?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: A snapshot captures existing state at a known log offset; a compacted log may itself retain latest state for every key and allow full rebuild by replay.

short_answer_questions.question: CDC vs event sourcing?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: CDC observes low-level mutations of an ordinary mutable DB; event sourcing models application intent directly as immutable events.

short_answer_questions.question: Why distinguish command from event?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: A command can be rejected; once accepted and emitted as an event, it is a durable fact that downstream consumers must accommodate.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain state as an integral of events.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Current mutable state results from folding the historical sequence of changes; preserving the log makes that state reproducible.

short_answer_questions.question: Why are immutable events valuable?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: They improve auditability/debugging, retain analytical history, support rebuilding, and allow multiple read views.

short_answer_questions.question: What problem does CQRS address?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: It lets the write model reflect events/commands while separate read models are denormalized and optimized for particular queries.

short_answer_questions.question: CEP vs stream analytics?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: CEP searches for event patterns/sequences using persistent queries; analytics computes aggregations and statistical measures over windows.

short_answer_questions.question: Event time vs processing time?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Event time describes when the real-world event occurred; processing time describes when the processor handled it. Lag/replay can make them diverge.

short_answer_questions.question: Why are event-time windows difficult?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: There is no definitive moment when all late events have arrived; systems need lateness policies, corrections, or producer progress markers.

short_answer_questions.question: Compare window types.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Tumbling = fixed/non-overlapping; hopping = fixed/overlapping; sliding = relative interval; session = inactivity-delimited.

short_answer_questions.question: Compare the three stream joins.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Stream-stream matches events in a window; stream-table enriches events with maintained reference state; table-table continuously maintains a materialized join.

short_answer_questions.question: Why are stream joins time-dependent?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Reference state changes over time and multiple streams lack a single cross-stream order, so replay may join an event against a different version.

short_answer_questions.question: What does effectively-once mean?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Retries may physically reprocess events, but visible state/output should be equivalent to one successful application per input.

short_answer_questions.question: Microbatching vs checkpointing?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Microbatching groups stream events into mini-batches; checkpointing snapshots continuously running operator state at barriers without forcing window size.

short_answer_questions.question: Why are external side effects the hardest part of exactly-once?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: The framework can roll back/retry its internal state but cannot necessarily undo effects already committed elsewhere.

short_answer_questions.question: How can idempotence replace distributed transactions in some cases?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Use output metadata such as source offsets so repeated replay is detected and produces the same final result.

short_answer_questions.question: What are the main stream-state recovery strategies?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Remote replicated state, local snapshots/checkpoints, compacted changelogs, or replay from input streams.

practice_problems.solution: 24, because partition assignment limits parallelism to the number of partitions.

practice_problems.prompt: Offset 500 is checkpointed. Consumer processes through 525 and crashes before next checkpoint. Which records may be replayed?
practice_problems.solution: Messages after the checkpoint, approximately offsets 501-525, may be processed again.

practice_problems.prompt: You create a new search index from CDC but retained changelog starts yesterday. What is missing?
practice_problems.solution: A consistent full snapshot corresponding to a known changelog offset, unless a compacted full-state log is available.

No; incrementing twice changes the result twice. Add deduplication metadata or transactional coordination.

practice_problems.prompt: Checkpoint succeeds, then email is sent, then process crashes before input offset advances. What risk?
practice_problems.solution: On replay the email may be sent again because the external effect was not atomically coordinated with input progress.

practice_problems.prompt: A 10-minute rolling aggregate loses local state. The full input log is retained. What simple recovery option may work?
practice_problems.solution: Replay the recent input events covering the needed window and reconstruct the aggregate.

beginner: Can define event, producer, consumer, topic, partition, and offset.
Can distinguish traditional queues from retained logs.
Can explain CDC, event sourcing, event time, windows, and idempotence.
intermediate: Can reason about acknowledgments/redelivery and duplicate processing.
Can explain CDC bootstrap and log compaction.
Can compare all four window types and all three stream join types.
advanced: Can design a replayable derived-data pipeline around a system-of-record changelog.
Can reason about time-dependent joins and historical reference versions.
Can design effectively-once processing with transactions or idempotent writes.
Can select a stream-state recovery strategy based on replay, snapshots, local state, and remote-state tradeoffs.

must_memorize: Batch input is bounded; stream input is unbounded.
Event = immutable record of something that happened.
Producer creates events; consumer processes; topic groups related events.
Slow consumer choices: drop, buffer, backpressure.
Traditional brokers often ack/delete individual messages.
Load balancing = one group member per message; fan-out = all independent subscribers.
Lost ack can cause redelivery and duplicate processing.
Load balancing + redelivery can reorder messages.
Log-based broker = append-only partitioned retained message log.
Offset totally orders events only within a partition.
Consumer-group parallelism is normally limited by partition count.
Retained logs support replay by resetting offsets.
Database replication log is itself a write-event stream.
Dual writes can race or partially fail.
CDC exposes one authoritative database ordering to derived systems.
CDC bootstrap = consistent snapshot + known log offset.
Log compaction retains latest value per key; tombstones represent deletion.
Event sourcing records domain-level immutable facts.
Command may fail; event is accepted and immutable.
Current state is a projection/accumulation of events.
CQRS separates write representation from read-optimized views.
CEP stores event-pattern queries; stream analytics computes windowed aggregates.
Event time is occurrence time; processing time is handling time.
Late events require explicit policy: ignore or correct/retract.
Tumbling = fixed non-overlapping.
Hopping = fixed overlapping.
Sliding = relative time span.
Session = inactivity-delimited.
Stream-stream = window correlation.
Stream-table = event enrichment from maintained reference state.
Table-table = continuously maintained materialized join.
Time-dependent joins need historical reference versions for deterministic replay.
Exactly-once is better thought of as effectively-once visible effects.
Microbatching processes small bounded chunks.
Checkpointing snapshots continuous operator state.
External side effects require atomic coordination or idempotence.
Idempotence means retry has same final effect.
Source offsets/IDs can provide deduplication metadata.
State recovery: remote store, checkpoint, changelog, or replay.
final_review.memory_chain: UNBOUNDED EVENTS -> PRODUCER/CONSUMER -> QUEUE/BACKPRESSURE -> ACK/REDELIVERY -> PARTITIONED LOG -> OFFSET/REPLAY -> DATABASE CHANGELOG -> DUAL-WRITE PROBLEM -> CDC -> SNAPSHOT/COMPACTION -> EVENT SOURCING -> COMMAND/EVENT -> STATE FROM LOG -> CQRS -> CEP/ANALYTICS -> EVENT TIME -> WINDOWS -> STREAM JOINS -> TIME-DEPENDENT STATE -> EFFECTIVELY-ONCE -> MICROBATCH/CHECKPOINT -> ATOMIC COMMIT/IDEMPOTENCE -> STATE RECOVERY
final_review.one_sentence_takeaway: Stream processing treats never-ending event logs as replayable data sources and turns them into continuously maintained derived state while explicitly handling time, ordering, retries, and failure.
